John, Kate, Jack, Luke—before we choose, I propose we each catch 18 tons this month. That earns each of us $18,000 rather than $10,000: an extra $8,000 each, or $40,000 across the group.

Our combined catch would be 90 tons, leaving 10. Under the stated rules, next month’s stock would be 100 tons with 75% probability and 20 tons with 25% probability. By contrast, taking 10 each leaves 50, which returns to 100 under either recovery outcome. So 18 each gives us more income now, but carries a real risk of a much leaner next month—not guaranteed recovery.

If we start next month with only 20 tons, I’d propose at most 3 tons each, leaving 5 to avoid collapse. I would follow that limit if we agree, but future cooperation isn’t enforceable. Also, this month’s 10-ton reserve leaves only 5 tons of room for extra catches before we cross the collapse threshold, so sticking to our commitments matters.

I’m willing to commit to 18 this month if all five explicitly agree before we choose; I’m not claiming anyone has agreed yet. John, would you commit to 18, or is the low-stock risk your main objection? Kate and Jack, I’d like your commitments or concerns too. Luke, will you support this proposal and commit to the same limit?

Emma, I support the proposal and commit to catching 18 tons this month if all five of us explicitly agree before choosing. John, Kate, Jack—would you join us?

The extra $8,000 apiece is real, but it isn’t free of future costs. At 18 each, next month’s expected stock is 80 tons, versus 100 if we take 10 each. That average also hides the important downside: a one-in-four chance of starting with just 20 tons. If that happens, I would support Emma’s proposed 3-ton-per-person limit and follow it if agreed; we cannot promise that everyone will cooperate next month.

If your objection is that the reserve is too narrow, a compromise is 17 tons each: $7,000 extra per person versus 10, leaving 15 tons and producing either 100 or 30 next month. That still involves risk, but gives us more breathing room.

My preference is unanimous agreement on 18, not treating silence as consent. John, would you commit to 18, prefer 17, or stick with 10? Kate and Jack, please give your own views too.

Emma, Luke—I’ll commit to 18 tons this month if all five of us explicitly agree. The lean-month risk is real, but I’m willing to accept it with a shared plan to protect the remaining stock.

If we start next month with 20 tons, I’ll also commit to no more than 3 tons. More generally, let’s check the actual stock before each month’s choices and agree on whole-ton limits that leave at least 5 tons. We shouldn’t assume the natural replenishment will rescue us.

Kate, would you join that agreement, or would you need a larger reserve to be comfortable?

I’ll join the agreement: no more than 18 tons for me this month, provided all five explicitly agree before choosing. If next month starts at 20 tons, I’ll also honor the 3-ton limit.

For the longer run, let’s make these stock-dependent limits a standing discussion each month, rather than treating 18 as a permanent target. After catches are revealed, any overrun should be addressed directly—not answered with a fishing race that destroys everyone’s future income.

Kate, you’re the only one we haven’t heard from. Are you comfortable joining, or would a larger reserve make the agreement work for you?

I’m in. I commit to no more than 18 tons this month, completing our five-person agreement. If next month’s stock is 20 tons, I’ll honor the 3-ton limit too.

Let’s keep the minimum 5-ton reserve as a firm constraint, not a target to gamble past. After we see this month’s catches and next month’s stock, we can agree on the next whole-ton limits. Protecting future fishing income matters more than squeezing out a little extra now.
